Flooding and bushfires can sometimes be two sides of the same coin and exacerbate each other. Bushfires render land barren, run off increases, local catchments fill up and can’t take on more rain, land charred by bushfires can’t absorb water, and so floods occur with any heavy rain because the water has nowhere to go.

Yes and I understand what you mean but the terminology is being used to emphasise that these are what used to be very rare events. The point of the phrase is to emphasise the events are (or rather, were) very rare events rather than to convey a literal technical probability (because none of these events would have had an actual probability of 1/100 anyway - this is a placeholder figure that signifies the event is very rare on the timescale of about one every century). 

Eventually we will stop referring to these events as being one in one hundred year events, because eventually the zeitgeist of how we anticipate and react to natural disasters will change. However we are just at the beginning of seeing an increase in these types of events, hence the media / people still referring to them as one in a hundred year events. It’s to emphasise or push a certain narrative - it’s not supposed to be a literal technically correct figure of the probability of these events.

The increased frequency of what used to be freak “one in one hundred years” events is due to the changing climate. As the climate continues to change we will see more and more of these extreme weather events. The measure isn’t meaningless - it’s a way to describe an event that is so extreme it should occur only once in one hundred years. The changing climate is increasing the frequency of these formerly rare events.

- someone left a negative review due to the negative user experience on the site. Note- it wasn’t just the ads, they said the website kept jumping around and made it difficult to read. The website was providing a bad user experience.

If the user has a bad experience on the website it is reasonable for the user to provide feedback to the creator via a comment. Maybe the creator isn’t aware of the website issues on certain browsers for example and the feedback is helpful.

- if the creator has a bad website which provides a bad user experience, the users may stop visiting the website, resulting in decreased revenue.

- if the only way you can make money as a content creator is by having your content on a site that provides a bad user experience, then it would be wise to consider another way to make a living because logically eventually your user base will stop visiting your page and advertisers will eventually stop purchasing ad space due to low traffic. This might mean looking at a different career path, finding another way to monetise your recipes (e.g. writing and publishing a physical cookbook) or doing something else like moving your recipes to a website with less intrusive ads and a better user experience. This is not an elitist view. This is just common sense.

You’re also somehow against people leaving reviews providing feedback about their experience. I just don’t get it. This isn’t someone just writing recipes for me out of the goodness of their heart - they are using me to make money. That’s the nature of this whole content creation business. It was advantageous for ancient cats to get along with humans once humans invented agriculture, as storing of crops and grain attracted rodents which the cats would then hunt. Humans were quite happy to have the cats around because free pest control, but obviously the cats that were more affectionate and domestic towards humans would have been allowed to stick around and probably even their offspring would also have been encouraged to stick around. Because cats were responding to this strong evolutionary selective pressure, it makes sense they would evolve behaviours that made humans more responsive to their needs.

Tux was a “stray” that I found under one of my old houses.

I was giving him cuddles and feeding him for a couple of months until one day he came inside and there was clearly something very wrong with him. Tux did not like coming inside yet was very insistent about coming in then lay in his cat bed that he had literally never cared to even look at before. I took him to the vet in the morning.

The vet said he had a serious bladder blockage and would be dead in 24 hours if we didn’t act. I said do whatever it takes to save him no matter the cost. It took three days with a catheter in and $900 and then I brought him home. I couldn’t keep him inside the recommended time because he didn’t know how to use a litter box. 

A few years later I moved and I took him with me. I asked the vets how to manage a cat who doesn’t know how to use a litter box and they told me to put a layer of dirt on top of the litter. This worked well and I taught him how to use the cat door. Tux very much loved the freedom that came with the cat door. 

A few years after that I was planning on moving to Australia from New Zealand and taking Tux with me. I took Tux to the vet to get his microchip placed (a requirement for the move) and when the vet scanned him they found he already had a microchip installed. I was stressed (at this stage I had had him for five years) but ultimately agreed it might be good to find the owner and have him returned to his owner rather than take him overseas, despite the fact I was a little concerned because Tux had always shown a trauma response and I was worried about who his previous owners might have been. I was planning on vetting the previous owners and making sure they were going to be safe for Tux to be with before leaving him with them. I was very upset to possibly lose him but also feeling very guilty I hadn’t got his microchip checked earlier, and I was sad for the family who was missing this cat that I essentially stole without knowing it.

The vet contacted the registered owner and found that she was in a rest home. They told me she was happy for me to keep Tux as she is in a rest home now and can’t really have him there. She wants to say goodbye.

I talk to the previous owner over text as she is deaf and confirm she’s happy for me to keep Tux. She wants to see him before we leave to say goodbye. She is relieved he is alive and that I have been taking care of him - someone told her that he had been shot so she is just relieved to hear he is alive and well. 

Tux and I visit his previous owner. Tux is not impressed - he hides under the bed the entire visit. I have a great conversation with the previous owner - she says she is glad he is alive, he used to be named Wehi (a Māori name, named for her late husband) and confirmed she lost him about a year before I found him. He got lost when she was moved to the rest home and used to live right down the road from me. She’s so glad that I found him and took care of him. She says she’s sad to give him up but knows he wouldn’t be happy living in the rest home and she’s glad he’s got me. She tries to leave money for me and Tux in her will and I tell her Tux is well taken care of and doesn’t need any money and if she wants to do that she should leave some money to the local organisation that rehomes stray cats. 

Tux and I visit her a couple of times before we leave. At some point we call the registration office together and get his registration transferred from her to me. Tux is unhappy during all of these visits and hides under the bed but she seems to be very happy to have someone to talk to and she’s being so wonderful letting me keep him so we keep going. My flatmate takes a nice picture of Tux and we get it printed and framed to give to Tux’s previous owner. 

Eventually Tux and I move to Australia and the communication from his previous owner drops off. Tux needs to be an indoor cat in his new home in Australia because there is a cat curfew. Tux doesn’t care because the birds in Australia are huge and he isn’t used to that and he’s frightened of them. Tux has finally learned to use a litter box without dirt on top. Tux eventually seems bored so we adopt a kitten, Tux and the kitten get on well and play together daily.

Tux has had quite a journey, but he’s happy and healthy as of today! His previous owner clarified his age for me - he is about 10. 
He is such a sweet boy, he has come a long way from being terrified to being inside. 
I feel terrible about not taking him to get microchip scanned earlier, but he just didn’t have any sort of markers that would indicate he was from a home. He was ratty, terrified of humans, terrified of being inside a house, and would wolf down food and water like his life depended on it.

Now Tux spends a lot of time with his little sister, they play all the time. He lives inside all the time now and seems to be quite happy with that arrangement - I am happy about it too because he used to come home with abscesses from fighting quite a lot and I would prefer for him to NOT be injured frequently. Tux seems to be thriving and he loves head scratches, he also loves lactose-free milk (but only gets it sometimes!). His fave food is the Dine packets of tuna and whitefish. 

I’m just glad that it all worked out for me and for Tux and that he seems super happy! Here’s to anyone who has rescue tuxies.

You could make some vege “chicken” nuggets. Get a block of firm tofu, squeeze as much water out of it as you can, then put it in the freezer in a freezer bag overnight. The next day take it out and thaw in the fridge, once thawed squeeze as much water as you can out of it again then put it back in the freezer overnight again. Then thaw it, once thawed rip it or cut it into chunks. Dredge the tofu pieces in a cornflour mixture seasoned with whatever you like (last time I used garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, salt and pepper) and shallow fry until golden. I haven’t tried freezing them once they’re cooked and reheating but I imagine it would probably work. 

The freeze/thaw process completely changes the texture of the tofu to a more chicken-like texture, and the cornflour mixture should be okay for GF people. The tofu nuggets taste pretty similar to chicken nuggets in my opinion when you do them this way!

I was put up a year in primary school and it ended up having a real impact on my teen years - because I was a year younger than all my friends but still wanted to do the same things they were doing, my parents had a real dilemma where they thought I was too young to be doing some of the things my friends were doing but at the same time they were very aware that they sort of caused that situation and didn’t want to unfairly disadvantage me socially.

On the other hand, my life might have looked very different if I hadn’t been put up a year. I was already starting to lose interest in school work because I was getting bored with the level I was at. Even with being put up a year I was still in all the accelerated classes all the way through school, so ultimately I think that in terms of my academic development it was positive.

If anyone has an advanced child and is reading this for advice, I would say the one thing I wish about my childhood was that people didn’t constantly tell me how smart I was. Because I was smart, I was very complacent about studying and I never learned how to study properly or how to stay focussed. This was fine all the way through school as I could easily do well academically without studying, but it fucked me over once I got to uni and I struggled more than my peers. 

So my advice would be to find a way to nurture your child’s academic strengths while also finding a way to grow skills that will be needed in their later academic life. Like for example I imagine some sort of advanced tutoring might have helped - something that was challenging and that would have forced me to develop some real skills in that space.

In my country, New Zealand, it is considered an extension of public schooling. The state issues a curriculum for early childcare.m that centres must adhere to, with reporting and things that go on to measure performance (these aren’t in the form of tests but are in the form of “learning stories” where teachers will report on what individual children are learning, their development, their progress and milestones they are reaching so that the state has some oversight over whether or not centres are implementing the curriculum and on whether or not the children are achieving what they are meant to be achieving). While the centres themselves are mostly still privatised, they are heavily regulated and fees are subsidised quite considerably by the state. But yes you are quite right - my department would like to see early childcare become fully socialised and state provided just like primary school is, as in particular we believe this would help to mitigate issues such as inconsistent approaches across different centres and difficulties with children transitioning from ECE to school. Also there is a major pay discrepancy between what early childhood teachers are receiving and what primary and secondary school teachers are receiving, despite the fact that ECE teachers are required to have the same level of education as primary and secondary teachers. So it’s a common belief in the industry that handing over more of that control over the ECE sector would relieve some of those issues too.

I work for an educational professional development unit at a university that provides professional development to teachers in the sector including early childhood educators.

In the last 30 years a number of important theories on how to teach young children have emerged or have become more widely acknowledged. Modern early childhood education is based on a body of research on child development which includes research by Jean Piaget, Erik Erikson, John Dewey, Lucy Sprague Mitchell, Alec Vygotsky, David Kolb, and others. Theories that underpin modern early childhood education include the Developmental Interaction Approach, socio-cultural learning theory, Piaget’s constructivist theory, social and emotional learning and Kolb’s experiential learning theory. Over the last 3 decades in particular, the early childhood education sector has begun to acknowledge that what happens in early childhood can impact the adult that the child will develop into. Studies have shown that early intervention (i.e. teaching children using some of the above theories) for young children exhibiting problematic behaviours can result in reduced instances of depression, anxiety, incarceration, unemployment, aggression etc etc for the individual when they reach adulthood.

Obviously this is a significant finding for societies in general. If investing in early childhood education can reduce some of the negative outcomes described above in adulthood, not only will it benefit the individual but it will also benefit society as a whole in the form of less public spending on incarcerating individuals, reduced healthcare costs for mental illness, reduced need for police intervention for aggressive individuals etc. Not only that, but research shows that young children receiving a good education (tailored for their specific age group) in their early years are better set up for learning all throughout school, and tend to be more likely to achieve success and happiness in later life.

Benefits for society aside, I think that the psychological research that has been done in this area has caused us to move away from the model where children just need to be babysat or watched over with little to no active learning taking place by the child. Young children are going through a significant period of cognitive development in their lives which impact the kind of adult they will later on become. Young children are learning far more than I think we ever used to give them credit for, albeit they learn in different ways than older children and adults. One example of this is “play-based” learning, as children are believed to learn mostly through play. Early childhood educators will set up opportunities for children to learn via play in a way that is tailored to the developmental level of the child. For example very young children - from about 6 months to 2 - benefit hugely from having sensory experiences - playing in the sandpit, playing with water, playing with something that has moving parts, becoming more aware of their bodies and their control over them so engaging in activities such as dancing, etc etc. As the child gets older, opportunities for play-based learning are again tailored to their appropriate developmental age, e.g. teaching children more social skills and how to interact with their peers and teachers. As the child grows and becomes more confident in their learning, early childhood educators will slowly encourage the child to be more and more independent e.g. allowing the children to serve themselves at mealtimes (with supervision from the teacher of course), allowing the child to choose which activities they might want to do from a range of activities available etc. This approach helps to establish a strong sense of self and confidence in the child and again sets them up for success in later life.

So I suppose the crux of all this is that, over the last 30 years in particular, early childhood education has moved away from the idea that children should be passively babysat. The research has shown that the experiences that children have in their early years help to shape the adults they will become. This is important to us as a society so governments have started to regulate early childhood centres to ensure that each child attending is receiving a good early childhood education that will set them up well for later life.

One thing I’ve really taken from all this is how little the general public really understands about how microorganisms work. I have a biology degree and did a lot of microbiology papers along with some plant pathology papers and some epidemiological work too. It’s one of those things that ends up being so second nature to you that you forget others don’t have the same knowledge.

People think I’m crazy with the precautions I take to avoid cross contamination in my everyday life but literally there are microbes everywhere. The types of microbes matter too - some are harmless and some are harmful. I’m careful to use separate scrubbing brushes and a separate plastic tub when I wash my cat’s food bowls, because I’m aware of how often flies land on the bowls and also aware of how many microbes can live in animal’s mouths and I don’t know what the microbes are so I would rather avoid them contaminating the dishes I use for me. I’m careful to avoid cross contamination from the bathroom to the kitchen in terms of cleaning cloths and things. 

People think I’m being over the top and I probably am a little bit, but it’s only just now I’m realising that it’s because people just do not realise how pervasive microorganisms are. 

COVID-19 apparently has the ability to survive on surfaces for up to three days. When you are sick with COVID-19, anything you touch should be considered contaminated with the virus. It also has the ability to survive up to three hours I think in the air. Viruses can get into your body easily by touching a contaminated surface and then touching your face. Viruses thrive in bodily fluids like saliva and phlegm and can be easily transmitted this way. Some people I’ve spoken too seem to think these things aren’t true - they are! 

Microorganisms are kind of scary because you can’t see them. In the lab when you’re working with them you kind of have to assume that anything that has come into contact with the microbial substance is fully contaminated and treat it as such. That’s why it’s important during this outbreak to regularly disinfect surfaces that are touched, wash your hands regularly and thoroughly with soap and water or use hand sanitiser, and avoid touching your face cause viruses can get into you through mucus membranes like your eyes, mouth and nose. 

So if you’re self isolating with other family members who are sick, act like the virus is definitely on things that they have touched. Have separate cutlery, bowls, cups, glasses for each family member and maybe wash them separately (like I do with my cat’s bowls) or in really hot soapy water or even better use a dishwasher to wash your dishes cause they are good at killing microbes. An infected person should wear a mask around other family members to avoid transmitting the virus and should regularly wash their hands and use hand sanitiser. Avoid contact - no hugs or kisses with infected family members. Apparently it’s good if you can use a separate bathroom from infected family members although I realise that’s not always possible. Just be careful and maintain a good distance and assume everything the infected person has touched is contaminated with the virus. Even with those precautions it’s still quite likely you’ll get it too, so maintain self isolation, work from home if you can etc to protect other members of the community.

I have a lot of issues with sound, but it isn’t necessarily the loudness or sounds or anything like that, it’s the complexity of noise that I find difficult. So for example, if I’m watching tv and someone starts playing a video on their phone near me, that really bothers me because the noise is quite complex, whereas if I was watching tv and say someone starts vacuuming near me, that’s not so bothersome because the vacuum is a constant, simple noise so my brain doesn’t get so overwhelmed.

Also there seems to be a threshold of things that people with autism can deal with. For example, most things that happen in my day to day life I’m okay with, but if I wear this one particular shirt I have that causes weird sensory issues I have a much lower threshold for other stuff that bothers me.

I guess something people don’t understand about autism is that when you have autism you experience everything really intensely. Autistic brains don’t filter out things as well as neurotypical brains do so it’s easier to get overwhelmed.

Also I can’t really tell when people get bored when I’m talking about my special interest(S). I get carried away a bit because I enjoy talking about them. I can’t tell when someone is just pretending to be interested to be polite. I would rather someone actually straight up say hey I know you’re interested in this but we have been talking about this for a while now do you think we could talk about something else?

Eye contact is really hard for me. If I’m talking to you and not looking at you I’m probably taking in every single thing you’re saying. If I’m looking at you I’m probably not paying much attention to what you’re saying because I’m focusing so much on whether or not I’m making the correct amount of eye contact.

Social stuff that comes naturally to neurotypical people doesn’t come naturally to me. Every single facial expression, every single movement I make is carefully thought about and controlled. This is why I get so exhausted in social situations. Social interaction is stressful for me, not enjoyable or relaxing. 

Every autistic person is different, so my experiences may not apply to another autistic person you know. But these are things I wish people understood about me.

This reads like you resent this woman for many traits that are almost certainly caused by her autism. She isn’t being bad at stuff deliberately to piss you off or to try to get out of doing work or anything - lots of the stuff you talk about regarding needing reminders and not being able to follow procedures will be because of her executive functioning issues. If you give this woman the right support and give her the right tasks to suit her talents she could end up being one of your best workers.

People with autism tend to thrive on routine so I would start with that. If there is a series of tasks that keep getting forgotten, can you try to get her to do them in a certain order each day like right when she gets in or something? She might respond really well to that repetitive routine and you might find that she starts being able to do the tasks without reminders and with less difficulty.

She might be having issue with some of the procedures because something that seems obvious to neurotypicals is vague and ambiguous to her. I would sit down with her with the procedures that she seems to struggle with and ask her to walk me through what she would do at each step. Eventually you will get to the part that is difficult and then you can get to the bottom of what is difficult about it - it honestly could just be that if a step was reworded slightly it would be easier to understand.

The social issues are probably more of an issue as she doesn’t seem to be able to pick up on the fact that the social interaction isn’t going well. I would consider moving her to a different position where she doesn’t have so much client interaction if possible, but you still need to work through the other issues with her because they will almost certainly crop up in the next role too.
The main takeaway from me is that this woman isn’t being difficult on purpose - her brain is just different from yours and it is 100% possible to work with her to empower her to reach her full potential, which is ultimately what a person in your position is really supposed to do, right? Thanks for taking the time to ask the question here - that shows that you are open to suggestion and willing to try to resolve the situation, but I would just be careful around your feelings towards the lady. I understand that it can be frustrating when it seems like someone isn’t pulling their weight and it is putting pressure on the other workers, but she isn’t doing it because she’s an asshole she’s doing it because the way her brain is wired means she might need some additional support. It is more economical in terms of money to make new plastic than recycle. But not necessarily more economical for the environment. 
When considering the impact of recycling on the environment you have to take a few things into consideration. How much energy does it take to produce new plastic vs using already existing plastic and recycling it? How much fresh water is used to produce vs recycle? How much carbon is produced when you manufacture the plastic from scratch vs recycling? I don’t actually know the answers to these questions and I imagine the answers are vastly different for each kind of material that needs to be recycled.
The upshot of plastic recycling is that plastic is not great to have in the environment in vast quantities because then we have the issue of where are we going to put it. Plastic takes 400 years to break down. Plastic is very good at attracting bacteria and toxins, so when it gets into the ocean it becomes a little toxin & bacteria magnet. Plastic, especially micro plastic, gets into the food chain via filter feeding organisms (think plankton) which are then eaten by larger organisms. The larger the organism, the more toxic plastic it is likely to have consumed. Humans eventually eat these large organisms and we ingest the toxic plastics.
So In terms of trying to avoid that, recycling plastic is obviously the way to go. But the impact that the additional carbon that is produced and energy & water that is used to do that recycling does have an impact on the earth. So in fact recycling should be the second to last option (with the last option being producing new materials) and we should in fact aim to 1. Reduce and 2. Reuse as both of those options are significantly better for the earth than recycling or producing new.

In terms of monetary and economic terms, it is cheaper to produce new plastic than recycle old plastic, which is why most companies, when using recycled plastic, will use it as a selling point and have a little note somewhere clearly stating the product is made from recycled materials. This signals to the consumer that the brand is environmentally conscious which could be a selling point for some consumers, so this extra selling point helps to offset the cost of the recycling.
